rounds.title: ROUND 3 · DROP
rounds.label: DROP
rounds.question: Which one cracks?
fact: 8 mm drop · standing: over half crack

explain.title: WHY?
lines: It flexes and soaks up the shock

source: Sutanto et al., Communications Physics (2025), MIT
Simulated test at published lab averages
caption: Standing egg vs lying egg 🥚 Squeezed: a tie. Dropped: not even close. Which one did you pick? (MIT, 2025) What should we test next? 👇 #egg #physics #science #engineering #satisfying #mythbusting #3d
description: We test the same egg two ways: standing on its tip and lying on its side. Most people expect the standing egg to be much stronger, because of the arch shape.

Squeezed slowly in a press, it's a tie. In MIT's lab tests, standing eggs cracked at 46.0 N on average (about 4.7 kg) and lying eggs at 45.2 N (about 4.6 kg). The difference is within the scatter between eggs.

Dropped, it's not close. From only 8 mm, far fewer lying eggs cracked. On its side the shell flexes more, like a spring, so it spreads the shock over a longer time and absorbs more energy before cracking. Strength (the load it can carry) and toughness (the energy it can soak up) are not the same thing.
The animation is a simulation using the lab averages from the study below.
sources_detail: Sutanto, Cohen et al., 'Challenging common notions on how eggs break and the role of strength versus toughness', Communications Physics 8, 2025 (MIT)
Static compression to first crack: vertical 46.0 +/- 6.6 N, horizontal 45.2 +/- 5.5 N; 46.0/9.81 = 4.69 kg, 45.2/9.81 = 4.61 kg
Drop tests 8-10 mm: horizontal eggs cracked far less often than vertical ones (more compliant -> absorb more energy)
